title: Zonal and ensemble statistics: how does it vary across zones and runs?
summary: Box plots of a measured quantity by zone along the flame, with the sample count under each zone and the zone mean of each repeat run drawn on top. It shows the trend along the flame, the spread within a zone and the repeatability between runs.

media.alt: Box plots of flame width for five zones from base to tip with sample counts under each, an orange median line, and five lines with markers for run means.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How does it vary across zones and runs?
read_the_figure.axes: x: zone (base, lower, mid, upper, tip), with n samples labelled under each. y: flame width in mm (0 to 24). Boxes: interquartile range and median; whiskers: range of the rest. Lines with markers: zone means of runs 1 to 5.
look_at: How does the median change from base to tip?
How does the spread (box and whisker size) change along the flame?
How far do the run means scatter around the box?
What is n in each zone, and is it the same?
read_the_figure.proves: A clear trend of median with zone and run means that sit near the boxes shows a repeatable spatial trend. Spread and n show how far the numbers can be trusted.
if_wrong: No n: a box from 5 points looks the same as a box from 500.
Run means scattered much wider than the box: the runs do not repeat, or each run mean uses very few samples.
Box plots of pooled runs: they hide the run-to-run variation unless the runs are drawn too.

terms.meaning: Box from the first to the third quartile with the median line; whiskers show the range of the remaining data.
Values below which 25, 50 and 75 percent of the data lie.
The set of repeated runs of the same experiment.
Standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample count; the uncertainty of a mean.
A region of the object (here an interval along the flame) over which samples are pooled.

remember: Box = Q1 to Q3, line = median, whiskers = range (here without outliers).
SE = s / sqrt(n); 95 percent interval about mean +/- 2 SE.
Show n per zone. Show runs separately from the pooled boxes.
A trend is only a trend if it is larger than the spread between runs.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along x is the zone (categorical), vertical position is the width. The teal box, the amber median line and the whiskers summarise all samples in the zone; blue lines with different marker shapes and dash patterns, one per run, give the mean per run so the run-to-run scatter is visible without relying on colour. The count n is part of each tick label.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Statistics per zone is a summary of many numbers by five: the box plot shows centre, spread and skew in one glyph, and placing the glyphs side by side makes the trend along the flame obvious. Overlaying run means separates two sources of variation: the spread of samples within a zone and the difference between runs.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: How does the median change along the flame? From about 6 mm at the base to 9, 12.7, 14.6 and 17.4 mm at the tip: it nearly triples. Q2: How does the spread change? The box of the base is only about 1 mm tall (whiskers 4.6 to 7.7), the tip's box 2.3 mm (whiskers 13 to 20): the spread grows with width. Q3: How repeatable are the runs? At the base the run means agree within about 0.5 mm; at the tip they range from about 15.4 to 19 mm, 3.5 mm. Also n falls from 64 to 40, so the tip is the least well determined zone.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: n per zone: the sample count is printed in each x tick label, which is the minimum needed to read a box plot honestly. A plot that omits it asks for trust it has not earned.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A box plot hides n: 40 samples at the tip and 64 at the base have different reliability, which is why n is in the label. Each run mean here uses only 4 samples per zone, so the run means scatter by about s / 2 = 1.2 mm at the tip, which is larger than the standard error of the pooled mean (0.4 mm). Whiskers are defined differently by different programs. Lines joining zones imply continuity between categorical zones. Few runs (5) make any estimate of run-to-run variance unreliable.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Violin or strip plots show the full distribution; a plot of mean with a 95 percent interval per zone is cleaner for a trend; a table of n, mean, standard deviation and standard error is exact; a mixed-effects model separates run and zone effects.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Replace the boxes by mean and 95 percent intervals, draw the intervals of each run, and print n, mean and s in a table under the axis.

steps.title: Standard error and a 95 percent interval
steps.note: For large n; use the t value for small n.

steps.title: Why run means scatter more than the pooled mean
steps.note: Averages over fewer samples are noisier by the ratio of the square roots of n.

worked.title: Uncertainty of the tip-zone mean
worked.problem: Tip zone: n = 40, s = 2.3 mm, mean 17.4 mm. Find SE, the 95 percent interval, and the standard error of a run mean based on 4 samples.
worked.answer: Pooled tip mean 17.4 +/- 0.7 mm (95 percent); a run mean from 4 samples is uncertain by 1.15 mm, which explains the scatter of the lines at the tip.

analyze.q: The base boxes are narrow and the tip boxes are wide. Does width scatter grow because the flame is unsteady there or because n is lower?
Why do the run lines cross each other between zones?

evaluate.q: Would you claim the runs are repeatable on this evidence?
evaluate.hint: Five runs, four samples per zone each.

create: Draw mean and 95 percent intervals per zone for each run in a different offset, side by side.
Add a column of n, mean and s below the axis.

checks.q: Why print n under each zone?
checks.hint: What does a box not tell you?
checks.answer: The box does not show how many samples it comes from; n shows how reliable it is.

checks.q: The tip box is higher than the base box by about 11 mm. Is this a real trend if the run means differ by 3.5 mm?
checks.hint: Compare the effect to the run-to-run scatter.
checks.answer: Yes: 11 mm is more than three times the run-to-run range of 3.5 mm, so the trend with zone is real even if the individual tip means are uncertain.
